name: Game Development
description: Game loops, delta time, ECS, physics, Unity/Unreal/Godot fundamentals and performance discipline.

modules.name: Engine Fundamentals
modules.description: The loop, time, and the architecture patterns games are built on.

cards.prompt: What does a game loop do, and why is physics usually on a fixed timestep?
cards.answer: Each frame: process input, update simulation, render. Physics runs on a fixed timestep accumulator so the simulation is deterministic and stable regardless of frame rate, with rendering interpolating between physics states.
cards.explanation: Variable-timestep physics behaves differently at 30 and 144 fps — collisions tunnel and integrators blow up. The standard structure accumulates real time and runs zero or more fixed steps per frame, which is Unity's FixedUpdate and Unreal's substepping.

resources.title: Gaffer On Games — Fix your timestep

cards.prompt: Why does this player move faster on a 144 Hz monitor?
cards.answer: The movement is per frame, not per second. Multiply by `Time.deltaTime` so speed is expressed in units per second and is frame-rate independent.
cards.explanation: Every per-frame change — movement, rotation, timers, lerps — needs delta time. The classic follow-up bug is `Lerp(a, b, deltaTime)`, which is frame-rate dependent smoothing; use `1 - exp(-k * dt)` when you need a stable exponential ease.

cards.answer: OO puts data and behaviour in deep inheritance hierarchies; ECS separates entities (ids), components (plain data) and systems (behaviour over component queries).

left.title: GameObject / inheritance
points: Intuitive: a Player is a Character is an Entity

cards.explanation: ECS exists because of the memory wall: iterating 10,000 positions packed in an array is far faster than chasing 10,000 scattered objects. Unity DOTS, Bevy and most modern engines lean this way for simulation-heavy code.

cards.answer: Unity: C#, huge asset ecosystem, strongest for mobile and mid-scale 3D/2D. Unreal: C++ and Blueprints, best-in-class rendering, AAA and cinematics. Godot: GDScript/C#, tiny, free and open source, excellent 2D.

left.title: Unity / Unreal
points: Unity: fastest iteration, biggest job market
Unity: royalty-free tiers, licence history is a real risk factor
Unreal: 5% royalty past a revenue threshold

right.title: Godot
points: MIT licensed — no fees, no rug pulls

cards.explanation: Pick by project shape and team skills, not by engine loyalty. Prototype in whichever you can iterate fastest with — the engine matters far less to a finished game than scope control does.

modules.name: Systems & Performance
modules.description: Collision, state machines, memory discipline and shipping something playable.

cards.prompt: How does collision detection avoid checking every pair of objects?
cards.answer: In two phases. Broad phase uses a spatial structure (uniform grid, quadtree/octree, BVH, sweep and prune) to find candidate pairs cheaply. Narrow phase does exact tests (SAT, GJK) only on those candidates.
cards.explanation: Naive all-pairs is O(n²) — 1,000 objects is 500,000 tests per frame. Broad phase cuts that to near-linear. The other classic issue is tunnelling: a fast object skipping through a thin wall, solved with continuous collision detection or swept tests.

cards.prompt: Your player controller is a thicket of booleans: isJumping, isAttacking, isDashing. What is the fix?
cards.answer: A finite state machine: one explicit state at a time with defined transitions. Each state owns its enter, update and exit behaviour, and impossible combinations become unrepresentable.
cards.explanation: N booleans give 2^N combinations, most of them invalid — that is where 'attacking while dashing while dead' bugs come from. Hierarchical state machines handle shared behaviour (all airborne states), and behaviour trees scale better for complex AI.

cards.prompt: Your bullet-hell game stutters every few seconds. What is the likely cause?
cards.answer: Garbage collection pauses from allocating and destroying hundreds of objects per second. Pool them: pre-allocate a fixed set, deactivate instead of destroying, and reuse.
cards.explanation: In a 60 fps game the entire frame budget is 16.6 ms, so even a 10 ms GC pause is a visible hitch. Pooling also avoids fragmentation and instantiation cost. Watch for per-frame allocations hiding in string concatenation, LINQ and boxing.

cards.prompt: What is the per-frame time budget at 60 fps and at 144 fps?
cards.answer: 16.7 ms at 60 fps, 6.9 ms at 144 fps — for everything: input, simulation, physics, rendering and presentation.
cards.explanation: That budget is the discipline of game programming. Profile before optimising — the culprit is usually draw calls, an unbatched material, an O(n²) loop over entities, or GC. Frame *consistency* matters more than average fps: a steady 60 beats a spiky 90.

cards.prompt: Why do most hobby games never ship, and what actually helps?
cards.answer: Scope. The fix is brutal reduction: build the core loop first, make it fun with placeholder art, and cut everything that does not serve it. Ship something small and finished before something large and imagined.
cards.explanation: Vertical slice over horizontal features: one complete level beats twelve half-systems. Playtest early with someone who has never seen it — you cannot feel your own game's onboarding. And engine work is not progress unless it is on the critical path.
